title: the crossing of the Yamuna
hook: on the far bank, a whole village is asleep, and Vasudeva has to leave his son beside a sleeping stranger

segments.voice: Yesterday the guards slept, the doors opened, Shesha's hoods sheltered father and child, and the river gave way. Your line was the river gives way.

Gokula is silent. Vasudeva comes up out of the river, soaked, with the baby in his arms, and walks into the cowherd village where his friend Nanda lives. Nobody stops him. Nobody even stirs. The Bhagavata says everyone in Nanda's household is fast asleep. Inside, Nanda's wife Yashoda has just given birth too. She lies beside a newborn girl, so deeply asleep that she doesn't know what kind of child she has had.
screen: `GOKULA IS SILENT.` → `NANDA'S HOUSE ASLEEP.` → `YASHODA AND A NEWBORN GIRL.`

segments.voice: He makes the exchange. He lays his son down beside Yashoda and picks up her daughter. Then he walks back the way he came: across the river, through the open doors, into the prison. He sets the girl down on Devaki's bed. The text says he put the fetters back on his own feet, and the doors closed, as if nothing had happened. This is the man who walked into a flood to save his son, and his journey ends with giving that son away, to a woman who doesn't know, in a house where he can't stay, and walking himself back into chains. The rescue only works if he goes back. And there is the girl: someone else's newborn daughter, carried into the prison where Kamsa killed Devaki's children. The Bhagavata has told us who she is: Yogamaya, the Lord's own power, born to Yashoda for exactly this. Vasudeva may not fully know. He carries her anyway. And Yashoda will wake up to a son. In the stories ahead she is his mother in every way they show: the one who feeds him, chases him, scolds him, and ties him up when he steals butter. A crossing usually means reaching the other side and staying there. This one means leaving the most precious thing on the other side, and coming home with empty arms.
screen: `THE EXCHANGE IN THE DARK` · `BACK ACROSS, BACK INTO CHAINS` · `THE GIRL IS YOGAMAYA` · then, large: `YASHODA WAKES UP A MOTHER`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you have had to entrust to other people: a child at school, a parent in someone's care, a friend far away, a project you handed over. Breathe in and see them safe on the other side; breathe out and let your hands open a little, caring deeply while someone else holds them. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer.
Yashoda. Krishna's foster mother in Gokula, who wakes beside him after Vasudeva makes the exchange and carries her daughter back into the prison.
Your line: he returns with empty arms. Tomorrow, a cry in the cell. Day eight hundred eighty-three, done.

screen: `DAY 883 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE CROSSING OF THE YAMUNA.`

howItsDone: Hindus honor Yashoda as Krishna's foster mother, and Nanda's household in Gokula is remembered in songs and festivals of Krishna's childhood; Nandotsava, the celebration in Nanda's village, is kept by some communities.

chat.meaning: He left his son with Yashoda, carried her daughter back, and put his own fetters on. The rescue only works if he goes back.

Gokula.meaning: the cowherd village across the river

Nanda.meaning: the cowherd of Gokula, Vasudeva's friend

Yashoda.meaning: Nanda's wife, who raises Krishna as her son

Yogamaya.meaning: the Lord's own power, born as Yashoda's daughter

Devaki.meaning: Krishna's birth mother, in Kamsa's prison

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.3.51–53: Vasudeva in Nanda's house, the exchange with Yashoda's daughter, the return to the prison
Bhagavata Purana 10.2.6–9: the Lord's instruction that Yogamaya be born to Yashoda

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm that Yashoda, overcome by sleep, did not know the sex of her child (10.3.53), and that the text has Vasudeva put the fetters back on his own feet.
'Vasudeva may not fully know' who the girl is: interpretive; the text does not say what he knew.
Nandotsava named in howItsDone with 'some communities'; a Keeper may adjust or cut.
The closing allusion to Yashoda tying Krishna up looks ahead to later stories (the binding, Bhagavata 10.9); the butter thief is day 887.
